Abstract 
It has been found that several circulating metabolites derived from gut microbiota 
fermentation associate with a systemic immuno-inflammatory response and kidney 
injury, which has been coined the gut–kidney axis. Recent evidence has suggested that 
short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which are primarily originated from fermentation of 
dietary fibre in the gut, play an important role in regulation of immunity, 
blood pressure, glucose and lipid metabolism, and seem to be the link between 
microbiota and host homeostasis. In addition to their important role as fuel for colonic 
epithelial cells, SCFAs also modulate different cell signal transduction processes via 
G-protein coupled receptors, and act as epigenetic regulators by the inhibition of 
histone deacetylase and as potential mediators involved in the autophagy pathway. 
Though controversial, an intimate connection between SCFAs and kidney injury has 
been revealed, suggesting that SCFAs may act as new therapeutic targets of kidney 
injury. This review is intended to provide an overview of the impact of SCFAs and the 
potential link to kidney injury induced by gut-derived inflammatory response. 
Key words: gut–kidney axis; inflammation; kidney injury; short-chain fatty acids

1. Introduction 
It is now established that renal immune and inflammatory processes play a 
primary role in kidney injury leading to glomerulosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis [1]. 
Recently, more and more data indicate that renal inflammation is associated with the 
bacterial load and endotoxin generated by gastrointestinal dysbiosis, which augments 
intestinal permeability and leads to the development of acute renal failure related to 
infection and acceleration of chronic kidney disease (CKD) [2, 3]. Therefore, an 
intimate connection between the gut and kidney has been proposed, which is called 
the gut–kidney axis [4, 5].  
One class of molecules that acts as a link between the microbiota and the 
immune-inflammatory response are short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), the main 
metabolic products of anaerobic bacteria fermentation in the intestine [6]. At present, 
SCFAs have been recognized as potential mediators involved in intestinal immune 
function [7]. Studies reveal that SCFAs can reach the bloodstream and act as a link 
between microbiota and the immune system by modulating inflammatory gene 
expression, chemotaxis, differentiation, proliferation and apoptosis [8]. In fact, SCFAs 
treatment has been shown to ameliorate inflammatory diseases in vivo, such as colitis, 
airway disease, and metabolic syndrome in diet-induced obese mice [9]. These 
beneficial effects of SCFAs were not only related to their property as histone 
acetylation (HDAC) inhibitors, but also related to their activation of transmembrane 
cognate G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and their modulatory effect in 
autophagy pathway [10, 11]. Studies have already attempted to investigate the 

--- Page 6 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
5
therapeutic effect of SCFAs in kidney injury both in vivo and in vitro. However, the 
mechanism of SCFAs in gut–kidney axis has yet to be fully explored. This review is 
intended to provide an overview of the role of SCFAs in gut-derived inflammatory 
responses and the effects of SCFAs on kidney injury.  
2. SCFAs and SCFAs-mediated responses 
2.1 Origin, production, transport, distribution and basic functions of SCFAs 
It is generally considered that SCFAs are produced by the bacterial fermentation 
of macro-fibrous material that escapes digestion in the upper gastrointestinal tract and 
enters the colon [6,12]. 90~95% of SCFAs in the colon are made up of acetate, 
propionate and butyrate, differences in the rate and ratio of these SCFAs production 
depend primarily on the type of substrate used as opposed to the composition of the 
intestinal microbiota [13]. However, under conditions of increased fat oxidation such 
as prolonged starvation and diabetes, endogenous acetate production predominates 
[14]. In addition, propionate, and to a lesser extent acetate, are produced 
endogenously from the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids and methionine 
[15]. These results suggest that impaired glucose tolerance and abnormal amino acid 
metabolism possibly results in increased endogenous production of SCFAs. 
More than 90~95% of SCFAs are absorbed by colonic epithelial cells as energy 
sources mainly through specific apical solute carriers such as the monocarboxylate 
transporter 1 [16] and the sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter 1 coupled to 
HCO3
− secretion [17], which maintain energy homeostasis and contribute 
approximately 5~10% towards human basal energy requirements [7,18]. Although 

--- Page 7 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
6
butyrate is rapidly used as an energy source for colonocytes, it is also important in the 
regulation of colonic cell proliferation, differentiation and in evoking hormone release 
by modulation of gene expression associated with improvement in metabolic health 
[19, 20]. However, most of the acetate and propionate enters the portal circulation and 
peripheral blood [16]. Propionate entering the portal circle is primarily utilized in 
gluconeogenesis in the liver, with subsequent metabolism to CO2 by the tricarboxylic 
acid cycle and other metabolic pathways; consequently a significant amount of acetate 
enters the systemic circulation and reaches peripheral tissues. The detailed 
physiological concentrations and composition of SCFA anions in human intestinal and 
blood contents are listed in Table 1 [13]. SCFAs exhibit tissue-specific physiological 
functions in response to such concentration gradients. The concentration of SCFAs in 
the gastrointestinal tract and blood may predispose to, or prevent, pathological 
conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), cancer and diabetes [9].  
2.2 Receptors of SCFAs 
About ten of the de-orphanized GPCRs have been identified as nutrient receptors, 
and of those, four have been identified as SCFAs receptors [21]. SCFAs show a 
distinct structure–activity relationship toward these GPCRs; the effect and function of 
the four major GPCRs related to gut-kidney axis responses to SCFAs are discussed in 
this section of the review.  
GPR41and GPR43 
GPR41, also known as free fatty acid receptor 3 (FFAR3) and GPR43 (known as 
FFAR2) have been attributed with intestinal chemosensing function involved in the 

--- Page 8 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
7
regulation of insulin secretion and appetite, suggesting a plausible mechanism in 
which luminal SCFAs signal satiety-related hormonal response and control energy 
balance [22, 23].  
It's worth pointing out that both GPR41 and GPR43 are expressed in kidney tissue. 
Gene expression analysis of SCFAs receptors reveales that there is no difference in 
GPR41 expression in kidney tissue induced by ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI), 
whereas level of GPR43 is increased after acetate treatment [24]. In view of the facts 
that the highest expression of GPR43 was found in immune cells, the regulation of 
immune function via GPR43 may be related to the metabolic beneficial effects by 
SCFAs [25, 26]. Moreover, recent investigation revealed an intriguing physiological 
function of SCFAs-activated-GPR41 on the modulation of blood pressure [27]. Since 
both inflammation and hemodynamic disorder are related to the pathogenesis of 
kidney injury, these findings have led to considerable interest in GPR41 and/or 
GPR43 as potential therapeutic targets for kidney diseases. However, many questions 
regarding their functions remain unanswered and controversial [28]; potent and 
selective tools will be required for future studies on GPR41 and GPR43. 
GPR109A and Olfr78 
GPR109A is firstly identified as a receptor for niacin and can be activated by 
β-hydroxybutryate and butyrate, but not by acetate and propionate [29]. It is found 
that the activation of GPR109A would inhibit nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) activation 
[30, 31]. A recent study showed that the beneficial effects of high-fiber diet involved 
activation of GPR43 and GPR109A in the gut epithelium, suggesting that GPR109A 

--- Page 9 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
8
and the nod-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome 
may help to promote gut homeostasis [32]. However, until now, a correlation between 
GPR109A and kidney injury has not been well understood. 
Olfactory receptors (Olfrs) are GPCRs that mediate the sense of smell. In 2009, 
Olfr78 and its human ortholog, hOR51E2, was initially identified in the renal afferent 
(but not efferent) arteriole of the renal juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), where renin 
is stored for eventual release into the bloodstream; Olfr78 was subsequently identified 
as a receptor for acetate and propionate, but not butyrate [33]. Ensuing research 
revealed that Olfr78 was co-localized with GPR41 and GPR43 in a variety of 
peripheral vascular beds [27, 34]. It is consistent with the idea that the contrasting 
responses of Olfr78 and GPR41/43 would produce a “buffering” effect to guard 
against wide swings in blood pressure [35]. Recent researches showed that Olfr78 was 
also expressed in the colon but was absent from other gastrointestinal compartments 
[36]; however, the metabolic effects of Olfr78 in colon and kidney are unclear to date, 
and it is expected that further analysis will elucidate its function in energy 
metabolism. 
2.3 Epigenetic regulation by SCFAs 
As well known, gene expression is regulated by the modulation of histone 
acetylation and HDAC. A study found that SCFAs may serve as non-competitive 
inhibitors of HDACs in that butyrate and propionate can selectively inhibit HDAC1 
and HDAC3 [37]. Butyrate is the most potent inhibitor of HDAC, with a maximum 
efficiency of approximately 80% inhibition of HDAC1/2, while propionate has 

--- Page 10 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
9
approximately 60% maximum inhibitory efficiency [38]. By inhibiting HDAC activity, 
SCFAs increase the acetylation of histone and reduce its compactness, consequently 
modulating gene expression, including NF-κB, myogenic differentiation antigen, p53 
and nuclear factor of activated T cells [39,40].        
The beneficial effects of the inhibition of HDAC are associated with their 
anti-fibrotic, anti-inflammatory, and immunosuppressant effects in obstructed kidney 
and was found to reduce cyst formation in polycystic kidney disease [41-43]. With 
regard to SCFAs, acetate treatment inhibited the activity of HDACs in AKI after IRI; 
sodium butyrate played a protective role in gentamicin-induced nephrotoxicity by 
inhibiting HDAC and increasing prohibiting protein expression [24, 44]. Therefore, 
epigenetic regulation may also be related to the beneficial effects of SCFAs on kidney 
injury; the use of such fatty acids as therapeutics is now in the realm of possibility.  
3. SCFAs involved in kidney injury induced by gut-derived 
inflammatory response      
3.1 Kidney injury induced by gut-derived inflammatory response 
Recently, the gastrointestinal tract has emerged as a major instigator of systemic 
inflammation associated with kidney injury [2, 45]. As shown in Figure 1, a single 
layer of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) are bound together by tight junctions, which 
not only constitute a physical barrier against the entrance of microorganisms, but also 
serve as active component of the host defense to prevent the systemic translocation of 
pathogenic microorganisms or their molecules into the portal circulation by sensing 
and responding to them [46, 47]. Commensal bacteria play an important role in 

--- Page 11 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
10
maintaining the intestinal epithelial barrier by enhancing the tight junction between 
epithelial cells and suppressing intestinal inflammation, and the intestinal immune 
system becomes largely tolerant to resident commensals [48, 49]. The disturbance of 
normal gut microbiota has been implicated in the pathogenesis of diverse illnesses 
such as IBD, obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and cardiovascular disease [9, 22].  
Recent evidences from studies on the AKI-to-CKD transition and ESRD indicate 
that changes of intestinal microbiota will occur in kidney diseases and rescuing 
microbiota dysbiosis may prevent toxins and pathogens across the intestinal barrier 
[50, 51]. Bacterial cell wall products such as LPS and peptidoglycans are potential 
cause of inflammation in patients with CKD [52]. It has been recognized in both CKD 
patients and animals that colon wall inflammation is associated with a breakdown of 
the epithelial tight junction barrier (“leaky gut”) and the translocation of bacterial 
DNA and LPS into the bloodstream (“gut-derived endotoxin”), and the underlying 
immune cells (such as macrophages, neutrophils and lymphocytes) are responsible for 
mounting an antimicrobial and inflammatory response [53]. Exposure to the 
endotoxin will initiate a systemic inﬂammatory response and oxidative stress, which 
will further induce and accelerate the kidney injury and cardiovascular disease, 
including AKI and CKD [51, 54]. The discovery of “gut-derived inflammation” 
strongly suggest that interventions aimed at establishing gut symbiosis and blocking 
microbiome-related pathogenic biochemical pathways should be explored to 
ameliorate kidney inflammation and uremic syndrome.  
3.2 SCFAs maintain intestinal epithelial barrier and inhibit gut-derived 

--- Page 12 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
11
inflammatory response  
How are endotoxins involved in gut-derived inflammatory response and kidney 
injury? Several intestinal diseases, in particular those involving mucosal inflammation, 
are thought to result from gut dysbiosis [9, 55]. An appropriate intake of dietary fibers 
is often believed to be associated with increased SCFAs that possess 
anti-inflammatory ability within the body, while a high-fat diet is shown to be 
correlated with a reduction of SCFAs and an elevation of LPS in the blood [53]. As 
discussed above, SCFAs can serve as energy source for the colonic epithelium [17-20]. 
Recent studies further demonstrated that SCFAs also can modify or inhibit the 
production of some cytokines and chemokines by IECs. It is observed that butyrate 
and other ligands activated GPR109A in IECs and then blocked basal and 
LPS-induced NF-κB activation thus suppressed colonic inflammation [30, 31]. The 
impairment of the immune response was associated with the absence of 
SCFAs–induced GPR41 or GPR43 activation in epithelial cells and a consequent 
reduction of inflammatory mediators in the colon in response to inflammatory stimuli 
[56]. In addition, the increased intake of SCFAs has the capacity to ameliorate 
parameters of intestinal inflammatory disease via inhibition of HDAC modulated IL-8 
and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) [57, 58]. Besides modulating 
inflammation, SCFAs also act on the epithelial barrier integrity. Studies found that the 
activation of GPR43 and GPR109A induced by SCFAs in IECs would increase the 
production of IL-18, a key cytokine for the repair and maintenance of the epithelial 
integrity; the incubation of IECs with butyrate was shown to increase transepithelial 

--- Page 13 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
12
resistance by promoting the assembly of tight junctions [59, 60]. Furthermore, SCFAs 
increase oxygen consumption by IECs, which obviously leads to a reduction in 
oxygen tension and results in a stabilization of hypoxia inducible factor [61]. 
Taken together, as summarized in Figure 1, these studies indicate that SCFAs are 
essential for the maintenance of intestinal epithelium physiology by regulating the 
cellular turnover and barrier functions and modulating the response after 
inflammatory/infectious/LPS stimulation. Although the mechanism behind these 
effects is not completely known, HDAC and GPCRs signaling pathway are implicated, 
and further investigation is required to fully clarify the role of SCFAs in gut-derived 
inflammatory response and kidney injury. 
3.3 Regulation of immunity and inflammation by SCFAs in peripheral tissue 
Oxidative stress and inflammation are inseparably linked as each causes and 
intensifies the other. SCFAs affect the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) 
and the phagocytic capacity of phagocytes [62]. Accordingly, therapies have been 
proposed to restore SCFAs production or to provide exogenous SCFAs in an attempt 
to reduce inflammation; actually, SCFAs treatment inhibited ROS production by 
improving mitochondrial biogenesis in a HK-2 human kidney epithelial kidney cell 
line after hypoxia [9, 24].  
SCFAs are also involved in leukocyte chemotaxis, affecting inflammatory cells’ 
migration and their several other key functions, and these effects may account for 
certain beneficial effects of SCFAs on tissue inflammation [63]. SCFAs, especially 
butyrate, were shown to inhibit macrophage migration in response to LPS [64].

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
13
Studies found that propionate and butyrate could suppress the production of 
pro-inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin 
(IL)-6 and nitric oxide, while butyrate could enhance the release of the 
anti-inflammatory cytokine (e.g. IL-10) and promote immune tolerance by 
lymphocytes [65, 66]. SCFAs treatment reduced the expression of the costimulatory 
molecules, CD80 and CD40, in bone marrow dendritic cells stimulated with LPS (20 
ng/mL in the presence of SCFAs), and also inhibited the capacity of these cells to 
induce CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proliferation [24]. Another mechanism of SCFAs on 
modulating inflammation involves in the downregulation of adhesion molecules on 
endothelial cells, which obviously results in the inhibition of leukocyte migration to 
inflammatory sites [67]. Despite the fact that most of the studies support the idea that 
SCFAs induce a tolerogenic and anti-inflammatory profile of T cells, evidences 
indicate that SCFAs induce Th1 and Th17 cells upon immunological challenges and 
also have the potential to induce inflammatory responses [68, 69]. Therefore, the final 
impact of SCFAs on immune system depends on the disease/model and other factors 
including time, route and concentrations of treatment used. 
4. SCFAs and signaling pathway cross-talk associated with 
gut-derived inflammatory response  
Inflammation is a complex process that reflects the local and systemic responses 
to different immunological and non-immunological stimuli. LPS and NF-κB are the 
two endings that widely investigated concerning their important role in inflammation. 
As shown in Figure 2, recognition of LPS by toll-like receptor-4 (TLR4) and its 

--- Page 15 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
14
cofactors triggers signaling through myeloid differentiation primary response 88 
(MyD88), results in the activation of NF-κB (the master regulator of 
pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines) and mitogen-activated protein kinase 
(MAPK), and will finally promotes the production of proinﬂammatory cytokines, 
chemokines, adhesion molecules and ROS [70,71].  
The molecular mechanisms through which SCFAs exert anti-inflammatory effects 
may be related to the activation of GPCRs and autophagy regulation. GPCRs activate 
heterotrimeric G proteins, where by α, β, and γ subunits are responsible for signaling, 
subsequently bound to β-arrestins (βarrs), βarr1 an βarr2, both of which regulate 
desensitization, internalization, intracellular signaling, and recycling of GPCRs and 
are positive regulators of LPS-TLR4-induced inflammatory signaling pathways, 
including NF-κB and MAPK [72,73].  
NF-κB signaling 
As shown in Figure 2, NF-κB was specifically studied and found to be reduced 
in most studies of SCFAs. Studies found butyrate exerts its inhibitory effect on NF-κB 
by preventing the proteasomal degradation of the ubiquinated inhibitor of NF-κB (IκB) 
[70]. Similar results have been recently reported by Park et al. [74]. It has been shown 
that βarr2 directly binds to and blocks phosphorylation and degradation of IκB, and 
finally leads to the inhibition of NF-κB activity. In addition, upstream kinases of IκB, 
such as IκB kinases (IKK) and NF-κB-inducing kinase (NIK), can interact with βarrs 
[75, 76]. Interestingly, NF-κB can be regulated by the GPR43-βarrs pathway, however, 
as far as we know, no report has linked GPR41 to βarrs. Recently, Lee et al. [77] 

--- Page 16 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
15
demonstrated that agonist-induced GPR43 interacted with βarr, with preference for 
βarr2, and knockdown of βarr2 would reduce the internalization of GPR43 after 
agonist ligation. Furthermore, the inhibition of NF-κB and the downregulation of its 
downstream genes, IL-1β and IL-6, by a GPR43 agonist were significantly 
compromised by the knockdown of βarr2. These results collectively suggest that βarrs 
may be involved in cross-talk between GPCRs and the NF-κB pathway, and GPR43 
and βarr2 might be promising targets for inflammatory diseases. 
MAPK signaling 
Although both receptors respond to the same group of ligands, GPR41 and 
GPR43 are coupled to different downstream signaling cascades. GPR41 selectively 
couples with Gαi subunit, which will inhibit the adenylyl cyclase pathway; so the 
activation of GPR41 induced by SCFAs will decrease the intracellular concentration 
of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) [21, 72]. On the other hand, GPR43 
couples with Gαi and Gαq, which may interact with proteins including adenylate 
cyclase, small G proteins (e.g., Rac and Rho), MAPK, protein kinase C, 
phospholipase C and phospholipase A2, ion channels and transcription factors et al.; 
therefore, GPR43 activation will attenuate cAMP production but augment 
intracellular Ca2+ and activate phospholipase C [73].  
Several studies analyzed the effect of SCFAs on the MAPKs pathway and 
suggested crosstalk between GPCRs and MAPKs pathways (Figure 2) [78]. Reports 
demonstrated that SCFAs or phenylacetamide-1 could elicit GPR43-dependent 
activation of protein kinase B and MAPKs (p38 and extracellular signal-regulated 

--- Page 17 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
16
kinase, ERK) in neutrophils in a p38- and Akt-dependent manner, and these responses 
were sensitive to pertussis toxin treatment, indicating the important role of Gi proteins 
participated signaling pathways in the movement of neutrophils in response to SCFAs 
[79, 80]. GPCRs-mediated activation of MAPKs is also regulated by the generation of 
intracellular messengers. There is a report indicated that SCFAs such as propionate 
could induce elevation of intracellular Ca2+ and mediate the phosphorylation of 
MAPK p38 via GPR43 [81]. Park and colleagues [74] demonstrated the inhibition of 
ERK-1/2 by three types of SCFAs (sodium butyrate, sodium phenyl butyrate, and 
sodium phenylacetate) has anti-inflammatory effects by repressing the DNA binding 
and transcriptional activities of NF-κB in IFN-γ-stimulated RAW 264.7 cells, whereas 
Diakos et al. [81] showed the inhibition effects of the three types of SCFAs on c-Jun 
N-terminal Kinase (JNK) but not NF-κB in mast cells. Further studies observed that 
GPR41 and GPR43 promoted activation of ERK-1/2 and p38 MAPK signaling 
pathways could induce the production of chemokines and cytokines during immune 
responses in cultured epithelial cells and mice after the administration of ethanol, 
2,4,6-trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid, or Citrobacter rodentium [82]. However, Bailon et 
al. [83] did not see an effect of butyrate on NF-κB, nor on the MAPKs, ERK, JNK or 
p38, in bone marrow-derived macrophages. The difference effects of SCFAs on 
MAPK signaling pathways may due to different cell types. It should be noted that the 
interplay between these pathways is either pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory, 
proliferative or anti-proliferative, depending on the expression of GPCRs and 
signaling intermediates such as βarrs [84], and these results suggest that GPR41 and

GPR43 mediated SCFAs signaling play an important role in their stress management. 
Autophagy  
Autophagy degrades long-lived cellular proteins and organelles, and plays an 
important role in maintaining physiological homeostasis [85]. There are evidences 
outline 
the 
crosstalk 
between 
SCFA-induced 
autophagy 
and 
apoptosis. 
Propionate-induced autophagy is associated with the inhibition of its major negative 
regulator, mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) [68, 86]. βarr1 and βarr2, as 
negative adaptors of GPCRs, mediate podocyte autophagic activity, indicating that 
β-arrestins are critical components that link renal injury to reduce autophagy in 
diabetic nephropathy [87]. Moreover, acetate treatment diminished the number of 
apoptotic cells in kidney tissue after IRI, but increased levels of autophagy-related 
protein 7 and mitochondrial DNA, which are involved in autophagy pathways [24]. 
These results suggest that acetate treatment is help to inhibit apoptosis via autophagy 
activation and targeting SCFAs may be a therapeutic pathway for countering kidney 
injury [88]. However, report concerning the direct relationship between SCFAs and 
the autophagy pathway in renal injury or kidney diseases cannot be tracked, and study 
on this area may lead a novel direction towards renal injury administration. 
5. Application of SCFAs in kidney injury  
Recently, albeit limited, studies have attempted to use SCFAs therapeutically in 
kidney injury in both animal and cell models, or explore the relationship between 
SCFAs and inflammatory conditions; studies involved in the application of SCFAs in 
kidney injury are summarized in Table 2.

18
AKI induced by IRI 
IRI-induced AKI is closely linked to the activation of tubular epithelial, 
endothelial, and immune cells by endogenous danger signals released after cell stress 
and death due to the enhanced production of ROS. Using a mouse model, 
Andrade-Oliveira V and colleagues [24] demonstrated that the SCFAs reduced kidney 
damage caused by IRI, with the greatest level of protection conferred by acetate. 
Moreover, mice treated with acetate-producing bacteria showed less susceptible to 
renal IRI than untreated controls. This suggested that acetate treatment diminished 
inflammation and injury in kidney epithelial and immune cells, and this modulation is 
most likely through inhibition of local and systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, 
cell infiltration/activation, apoptosis, autophagy, and chromatin modification. 
Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) 
CIN is a form of AKI following exposure to contrast media, which may involve 
the generation of ROS [89]. Machado et al. [90] showed that sodium butyrate 
treatment was associated with a decrease in levels of lipid peroxidation and IL-6 as 
well as tubular damage in a CIN model, but not protein oxidation. These effects were 
probably mediated, in part, by a decrease in the activation of NF-κB in the kidney, but 
not by any alteration in the phosphorylation of vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein 
content. These results suggest that sodium butyrate can inhibit NF-κB nuclear 
translocation, protecting kidneys from CIN mainly by inhibiting inflammatory and 
oxidative tubular damage, but not blood flow. 
Gentamicin-induced nephrotoxicity 

--- Page 20 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
 
19
Recent studies postulated that ROS, particularly superoxide anion radicals, are 
involved in the nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity of gentamicin [91]. The effect of acute 
and chronic treatment of various doses of sodium butyrate on nephrotoxicity induced 
by gentamicin was assessed, Sun et al. demonstrated that chronic treatment with 
sodium butyrate significantly attenuated gentamicin-induced nephrotoxicity by 
increasing the activities of superoxide dismutase, catalase and reduced glutathione; 
furthermore, sodium butyrate enhanced renal antioxidant enzymes activity [44]. These 
results suggest that sodium butyrate might be a potential candidate agent against 
gentamicin-induced nephrotoxicity. 
Ureteritis and Hydronephrosis 
As previously described, the functions of SCFAs in regulating immune cells, 
including T cells, appear complex and controversial. Park et al. [92] showed that oral 
administration of all major SCFAs, when chronically increased with higher than 
physiological levels in vivo, would generate Th1 and Th17 cells, induce tissue 
inflammation in ureteral tissues, and lead to kidney hydronephrosis in mice. Further 
research found that SCFAs-induced inflammation development is dependent on 
mammalian target of rapamycin activation, T cell–derived inflammatory cytokines 
such as IFN-γ and IL-17, and gut microbiota. Interestingly, scholars observed in this 
study that young or male animals were more susceptible than old or female animals, 
and GPR41 or GPR43 deficiency did not affect these SCFAs-induced inflammation 
development. Although the underlying mechanism is not fully understood, it is no 
doubt that non-receptor elements participated in these effects.

Taken together, despite the growing interest in SCFAs, many questions regarding 
their functions involved in acute and chronic kidney injury remain unanswered and 
controversial. It must be pointed out that the physiological concentrations of SCFAs 
in colon look quite different from peripheral circulation, and peripheral concentrations 
of propionate and butyrate are in the low micromolar range (Table 1). Most of the 
anti-inflammatory mechanistic studies that are discussed at present have been 
performed with mM concentrations in vitro, gut or kidney; this may have important 
consequences for translation of these results to physiological condition, particularly in 
kidney tissue. Therefore, an exploration of the larger concentration range of SCFAs in 
various kidney diseases, such as diabetic nephropathy, the leading cause of ESRD, is 
necessary. This knowledge may resolve some of these controversies by allowing us to 
identify the pharmacological concentration and genuine functions of SCFAs in kidney 
tissue, be it pro- or anti-inﬂammatory. 
6. Conclusion  
Gut microbial interactions with dietary fiber and the resulting SCFAs are 
important energy sources and signaling molecules. It is becoming increasingly 
accepted that exogenously administered SCFAs may be beneficial for human health. 
As summarized in Figure 3, receptors recognizing SCFAs and inhibition of HDACs 
play an important role in host (patho)physiology, such as regulation of endocrine 
system and metabolism, regulation of immune system and inflammation, and 
modulation of blood pressure; because of the promiscuous nature between microbial 
metabolites and host targets, these SCFAs might be able to exert broader impact on

host pathophysiology. But it will be a major challenge to identify the exact role of 
SCFAs in host (patho)physiology and to pinpoint their precise mechanisms, which can 
differ between tissues and even within the same tissue, depending on the cell type and 
stimulus concentration.  
Considering gut-derived inflammatory response and gut-kidney axis are important 
cause of kidney injury, here, we discussed how SCFAs are synthesized, distributed, 
and played the role in host (patho)physiology within the gut and in kidney. However, 
all the concerned studies are either preliminary or controversial. It is time for carrying 
out systemic clinical and basic research to fully understand the role of SCFAs in 
kidney injury.

Figures and figure legends 
Figure 1 
 
Fig. 1. The role of SCFAs in dysbiotic gut microbiota and gut-derived 
inflammatory responses. Changes in the intestinal microbiota reduce tight junction 
proteins of intestinal epithelial cells, allowing LPS to enter the bloodstream 
(endotoxin), which contributed to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines that 
define a state of gut-derived inflammation. However, SCFAs in colonocyte maintain 
and promote epithelial barrier integrity and prevent pathogen colonization; 
on the other hand, SCFAs are transported into the circulation via monocarboxylate 
transporter (MCT) to reach peripheral circulation and kidney tissue, and seem to exert 
broad anti-inflammatory activities. The discovery of the role of SCFAs in gut-derived 
inflammatory responses has created new therapeutic opportunities for kidney injury 
and other complications.

Figure 2 
 
Fig. 2. SCFAs take part in the regulation of LPS-TLR4-induced NF-κB and 
MAPK inflammatory signaling pathways. Generally, GPCRs are phosphorylated 
and then transduce a signal, subsequently bound to β-arrestins and lead to the 
internalization and desensitization of GPCRs. Agonists (SCFAs or synthetic 
agonists)-induced GPR43 interact with β-arrestins and induced the downregulation of 
NF-κB downstream genes; in addition to inhibitor of NF-κB (I-κB), IκB kinases (IKK) 
and NF-κB-inducing kinase (NIK) also crosstalk with β-arrestins. The binding of 
agonists to GPCRs also regulates several intracellular pathways, including MAPKs 
(ERK, JNK, p38). These studies suggest that SCFAs-GPCRs-β-arrestin signaling is a 
promising target for LPS-TLR4-induced inflammation (such as kidne injury) via the 
regulation of NF-κB and MAPKs.

Fig. 3.  SCFAs-mediated biological effect: a new pathogenesis and drug target of 
kidney injury. SCFAs play an important role in regulating the host homeostasis, not only 
via improving the intestinal environment, but also via GPCRs (GPR41, GPR43, 
GPR109A) and inflammatory signaling cross-talk in various peripheral tissues; 
SCFAs are also involved in the regulation of epigenetics (inhibition of HDAC), 
arterial blood pressure (Olfr78 and GPR41), and autophagy pathway; all these aspects 
are closely related to kidney injury. The current prospects for SCFAs interventions 
look interesting and have made the preliminary achievement; however, additional 
research is necessary to identify the pharmacological concentration and genuine 
functions of these SCFAs in kidney tissue.
